books.section: Topic 6.11 Reform in the Gilded Age

primary_sources: The Hull House, Chicago postcard, V.O. Hammon, early 1900s

stimulus.text: A color postcard titled “The Hull House, Chicago” shows a large complex of red-brick buildings, three and four stories high, with many windows, chimneys, and gabled roofs. The buildings fill a whole city block along a paved street with sidewalks, young trees, and a street lamp. No people are visible in the street. The postcard dates from the early 1900s and shows the settlement as it had grown by then.
stimulus.source_note: Vintage V.O. Hammon (Chicago) postcard of Hull House, early 1900s. Public domain; image viewed by the writer (shared pool: u6/5s24-exam1-mcq-01.jpg). The postcard dates from after 1898 and shows the settlement as it had grown by the early 1900s; the full complex shown was complete around 1911–1912, and a surviving dated example of this postcard is June 1, 1915 (Eastern Illinois University Booth Library). Hull House itself opened in 1889.

parts.prompt: Identify what the postcard shows about the scale of Hull-House.
parts.modelAnswer: The postcard shows that Hull-House had grown into a large multi-building complex filling a whole city block, with three- and four-story brick buildings. A single house had become a small campus in the neighborhood.

scoring.criterion: Earns the point for identifying the scale shown, such as a large complex of several buildings filling a city block.
scoring.notEarned: Calling Hull-House a single small house does not earn the point.

parts.prompt: Explain one way the postcard shows that Hull-House had become an established institution by the early 1900s.
parts.modelAnswer: The postcard shows a large permanent complex of brick buildings filling a whole city block, with paved streets, sidewalks, and a street lamp. That scale and permanence show a settlement that had put down roots and grown from a single house into a fixture of its neighborhood.

scoring.criterion: Earns the point for explaining permanence or scale as evidence of an established institution, such as several brick buildings filling a city block, or a paved street with sidewalks and a lamp.
scoring.notEarned: Describing the buildings without explaining what their scale shows about the settlement does not earn the point.

parts.prompt: Evaluate the extent to which this postcard is useful evidence about how settlement houses served immigrants.
parts.modelAnswer: The postcard is useful only in a limited way: it shows how large and permanent Hull-House had become, but it shows no people, no classes or services, and no immigrant residents. A student can learn how big the settlement grew, but not what it did for its neighbors.

scoring.criterion: Earns the point for a judgment weighing what the postcard shows, its size and permanence, against what it cannot show, the people served and the services offered.
scoring.notEarned: Describing the postcard without judging how far it serves as evidence about settlement work does not earn the point.
